title: SYSK Selects: How Condoms Work
summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of the December 2012 episode "How Condoms Work." After opening banter about a traffic ticket, Measure B in Los Angeles County, and the porn industry, the hosts trace condom history from prehistoric sheaths and ancient garments through Roman use, syphilis prevention in the Age of Exploration, animal-membrane condoms, Charles Goodyear's vulcanization, and Frederick Killian's dipped latex condoms. They cover condom dimensions and lubricants, manufacturing and quality testing (burst, leak, and electrical tests), disposal, proper use steps, effectiveness against pregnancy and STIs, teen condom studies, social marketing and global distribution (Thailand, UNAIDS), and niche products such as female condoms, spray-on condoms, anti-rape condoms, and the oral goat device. Listener mail closes the episode.
topics: Measure B Los Angeles porn condoms

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a SYSK Selects pick from December 2012. Josh and Chuck chat about a speeding ticket and about Measure B, the Los Angeles County referendum requiring condoms in porn, and the porn industry's reaction. Josh recounts scouting a porn studio set.

segments.title: Early condom history and wartime boom
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how condom use became widespread only recently, tied to HIV in the 1980s, with an earlier boom after the Great War to prevent venereal disease among soldiers. Penicillin and the pill reduced condom use until AIDS.

segments.title: Ancient penis sheaths, Roman use, and syphilis
segments.summary: The hosts describe prehistoric cave paintings and ancient sheaths in Egypt, Greece, India, and Japan, plus Roman-era contraceptive use. By Shakespeare's time condoms were common, mainly to prevent syphilis brought back by Age of Exploration sailors.

segments.title: Animal membrane and vulcanized rubber condoms
segments.summary: By the mid-1700s condoms were made from animal intestine membranes, which are porous and not protective against HIV. Charles Goodyear's 1839 vulcanization process made rubber condoms that were thicker and rougher and had to be fitted by a doctor.

segments.title: Latex dipping and modern condom materials
segments.summary: Frederick Killian developed making condoms by dipping glass molds into latex, producing thinner and stronger condoms. The hosts discuss latex ingredients such as zinc oxide, sulfur, and antibacterial compounds, and why latex condoms do not break down easily.

segments.title: Condom dimensions, lubricants, and spermicides
segments.summary: The hosts describe standard condom length, width, and thickness, the powders used in packaging, and lubricant choices. Nonoxynol-9 spermicidal lube is found to be ineffective with condoms and can irritate the vagina.

segments.title: Condom manufacturing, washing, and quality testing
segments.summary: Latex is collected in Brazil, Southeast Asia, or West Africa, mixed, dipped onto formers, vulcanized in an oven, washed, and tested for breakage and leaks using water-fill, electrical current, and dry tests. Slippage is considered user error.

segments.title: Condom disposal
segments.summary: The hosts explain that condoms should not be flushed because they do not break down and can clog sewer pipes. Advice is to wrap them in tissue and put them in the trash, and they mention condom litter on New York City streets.

segments.title: How to use a condom correctly
segments.summary: Steps include proper storage away from heat and wallets, checking the expiration date, opening without teeth, identifying the correct side, pinching the reservoir, unrolling to the base, using water-based lube, holding the rim on withdrawal, and not double-bagging or reusing condoms. Breakage is more likely if a condom was inflated or filled with water before use.

segments.title: Condom effectiveness, teens, and social marketing
segments.summary: Studies cited show correct condom use is highly effective against HIV and pregnancy, though typical use is less so. A teen study found condoms did not increase partners. Social marketing in Thailand and global distribution efforts by governments and the UN are covered, along with condom shortages and the taboo around condoms in some religions.
